title: The lowest of all
hook: whoever knows himself lowest of all is counted highest (Sukhmani 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahankaar: pride of power, of youth, of wealth, even of good deeds, and every pedestal has a drop. Today the same ashtpadi turns the ladder upside down.

Sikh tradition tells of an old man who carried water. Every morning before dawn, for years, he walked to the river, filled a pitcher, and brought it back for his teacher, Guru Angad, to bathe. One dark, stormy morning he tripped near a weaver's house and fell into the pit where the loom stood. The weaver's wife heard the noise and said, more or less: that's only Amru, the man with no home, who wanders around after his guru. A nobody. That nobody became the third Guru, Guru Amar Das.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CARRIES WATER.` → `HE FALLS. ONLY AMRU, A NOBODY.` → `THE NOBODY BECOMES THE THIRD GURU.`

segments.voice: Later in the twelfth ashtpadi, after the prides have been named, Guru Arjan turns the ladder over. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa. Whoever knows himself to be low is counted the highest of all. Neechaa: low, beneath. Oochaa: high, above. Ordinary Punjabi, words for a shelf or a hill. The verb in the middle matters: ganeeai, is counted, is reckoned. The line doesn't say the humble person feels high, or gets promoted at work. It says that in the real reckoning, God's count, the order is reversed. The next line deepens it: the one whose mind becomes the dust of all recognizes the Name in every heart. That's why the low place works: when you're not looking down on anyone, you can finally see what's in them. Back to the story. Tradition says when Guru Angad heard what the weaver's wife had called Amar Das, the homeless one, he called him the home of the homeless. The insult became a title. Tradition says Amar Das was already an old man when he became Guru, and asked everyone who came to see him, even, in the story, the emperor Akbar, to eat first in the langar, in the same rows as everyone else. The lowest seat, made into the door. So this isn't a trick for getting ahead. The stanza describes how things are already counted. We just can't see the scoreboard.
screen: `NEECHAA: LOW. OOCHAA: HIGH.` · `COUNTED, NOT FELT.` · `THE DUST OF ALL SEES EVERY HEART.` · `HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · then, large: `LOWEST IS HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose day you could make easier, a roommate, a coworker, someone at home, and one small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: the dishes, a refilled water jug, a door held. Picture yourself doing it and walking away without a word, and let that feel like enough.
Neechaa, low, beneath. Whoever knows himself neechaa is counted highest, the way an old water carrier became the third Guru.
Your line: lowest is highest. The homeless one became the home of the homeless. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water for Guru Angad as a model of seva, and in gurdwaras today volunteers wash dishes, sweep and mind shoes, often without anyone knowing their names.

original.note: Gurmukhi: neechaa, low; paired in the line with oochaa, high.

what a scholar hears: the verb is ganeeai, is reckoned, a word of counting and accounts, so the line is about how God keeps score.

far away, out of reach of others
hidden, kept quietly out of sight

chat.says: Isn't being humble just a clever way to get ahead later?
options: No. Sukhmani says the one who knows himself low is already counted highest; it's no trick.
Yes, the stanza promises that the humble will soon be promoted and honored by people.
Humility means looking down on proud people, since you know you're better than they are.
chat.meaning: Whoever knows himself neechaa is counted highest: ganeeai, counted, in God's reckoning, not promoted at work.

Guru Amar Das.meaning: the third Sikh Guru, once a humble water carrier

Akbar.meaning: a Mughal emperor who, the story says, ate in the langar

notes: aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa and jaa kaa man hoi sagal kee reenaa: confirm both lines sit at the end of ashtpadi 12 stanza 1 (Ang 278) and the transliteration.
The weaver's pit story, nithaavaan, and Guru Angad's reply (nithaaviaan da thaan, nimaaniaan da maan): tradition, not Gurbani; confirm wording and sources.
Guru Amar Das's age at becoming Guru (traditionally about 73) and the 'pehle pangat, peechhe sangat' langar tradition including Emperor Akbar: confirm.
